% A minipage cannot break across leaves: it overruns in silence. So every unit is
% boxed, its height written out, and only then set — python compares the height
% against \textheight. This is the measurement the mirror got from page marks.
\newcommand{\originals}[3]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\noindent
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2
    \end{minipage}\hfill
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue
      \setnoted{}#3
    \end{minipage}\par}%
  % ⚠ \ht0 ALONE IS WRONG HERE and silently reported ~5.7pt for every Part I
  % verso until 2026-08-09. This vbox's content is ONE LINE of two tall boxes, so
  % its height is just that line's height above the baseline and the whole column
  % sits in the DEPTH. Measure ht+dp. (\originalsone and \enleaf are multi-line
  % vboxes and were never affected.)
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\dp0\relax}\box0}

\newcommand{\originalsone}[3]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\ht0}%
  \ifthenelse{\equal{#3}{epigraph}}{\dropto{0.16}\box0}{\box0}}

\newcommand{\enleaf}[3]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\small\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H E #1 \the\ht0}%
  \ifthenelse{\equal{#3}{epigraph}}{\dropto{0.16}\box0}{\box0}}

% ---- the two foot-bands -------------------------------------------------
% The Loeb leaves roughly 44% of every leaf empty, and a Loeb's foot is where an
% apparatus belongs. The verso band carries the apparatus criticus against the
% originals; the recto band carries explanatory notes against the English.
%
% ⚠ The band is set at the FOOT, which means the leaf must be composed as a box
% of exactly \textheight with \vfill between body and band. \vfil alone will not
% do it: the preamble sets \raggedbottom, whose own bottom glue competes with it
% and lands the band a third of the way up. Same trap as the display leaves.
%
% ⚠ The band is measured INTO the fit record (\dimexpr body + band), not beside
% it. A band that overruns is exactly as silent as a minipage that overruns, and
% the point of the instrument is that nothing is unmeasured — which is how Part
% I's verso went 131 leaves without ever being tested.
% ⚠ The \par after the rule is load-bearing: without it the rule is just an inline
% box and the band's first word sets on the same line as the rule.
\newcommand{\bandrule}{\par\vspace{5pt}%
  {\noindent\color{rulegray}\rule{0.28\textwidth}{0.4pt}\par}\vspace{3.5pt}}

\newcommand{\apparatusband}[1]{%
  \bandrule{\scriptsize\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}\setlength{\parskip}{1pt}%
    \raggedright #1\par}}

\newcommand{\notesband}[1]{%
  \bandrule{\footnotesize\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}\setlength{\parskip}{2pt}%
    #1\par}}

% Compose a leaf whose body sits at the top and whose band sits at the foot.
\newcommand{\bandleaf}[2]{\vbox to \textheight{#1\vfill#2}}

% #5 = the Latin column's own noted lines, #6 = how many romans the Greek column
% already spent, so the series runs on rather than restarting at i.
\newcommand{\originalsn}[6]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\noindent
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2
    \end{minipage}\hfill
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      % ⚠ numbered on ITS OWN count — see the preamble. It is NOT reliably
      % line-for-line with the Greek: 20 of Part I's 131 openings differ, by as
      % much as six lines, because the plate turns its own long lines.
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}%
      \setnotedcol{#5}{#6}\plreset\plnumtrue #3
    \end{minipage}\par}%
  \setbox2=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\apparatusband{#4}}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\dp0+\ht2+\dp2\relax}%
  \bandleaf{\box0}{\box2}}

\newcommand{\originalsonen}[4]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \setbox2=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\apparatusband{#4}}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\ht2+\dp2\relax}%
  \bandleaf{\box0}{\box2}}

\newcommand{\enleafn}[4]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\small\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \setbox2=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\notesband{#4}}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H E #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\ht2+\dp2\relax}%
  \bandleaf{\box0}{\box2}}

% Place a display block a fixed way down the leaf. NOT \vfil: the preamble sets
% \raggedbottom, whose own bottom glue competes with any \vfil pair and lands the
% block about a third of the way down by accident. A title page sits where it is
% put, so put it.
\newcommand{\dropto}[1]{\vspace*{#1\textheight}}

% A leaf composed as one box of exactly the text height, so \vfill inside it
% divides the leaf instead of competing with \raggedbottom's bottom glue.
\newcommand{\fullleaf}[1]{\thispagestyle{empty}%
  \vbox to \textheight{#1}\clearpage}

% A display leaf: the 1853's own title and half-title pages, which are not running
% text and must not be set as though they were. \pl is redefined to drop its
% indent and centre, so the fragment renders as the page it is.
\newcommand{\titleleaf}[2]{\thispagestyle{empty}%
  \dropto{0.28}%
  \begingroup\centering
    \renewcommand{\parasep}{\par\vspace{2.4\baselineskip}}%
    \renewcommand{\pl}[2]{\par{\Large\scshape ##2}}%
    #2\par
  \endgroup}

\enleafn{2}{\input{fragments/en002}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Luke xviii. 1 — \emph{men ought always to pray, and not to faint} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,1 Thess. v. 17 — \emph{pray without ceasing} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Dan. vi. 10 — Daniel kneeling three times a day, as he did aforetime \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxix. 164 — \emph{seven times a day do I praise thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Gen. xxiv. 63 — Isaac going out to meditate at the eventide \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxix. 62 — \emph{at midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ex. xx. 24 — \emph{in all places where I record my name I will come unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxi. 1 — \emph{in the assembly of the upright, and in the congregation}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{The canonical hours, built out of Scripture rather than out of a breviary.} \emph{Seven times a day do I praise thee} sets the number, and each of the seven is then given a text that shows somebody praying at that hour: Mark's \emph{a great while before day}, the psalmist's morning watches, the third hour at Pentecost, Peter's sixth hour on the housetop, the ninth hour at the Beautiful Gate, Isaac at eventide, the night watches — with midnight added from the same psalm that set the number. \textbf{The office is being derived, not inherited}, and that is the argument of the whole opening.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{4}{\input{fragments/en004}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Matt. vi. 6 — \emph{enter into thy closet, and shut thy door} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Acts x. 9 — Peter praying on the housetop \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Acts iii. 1 — Peter and John going up into the temple \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Acts xxi. 5 — kneeling down on the shore, at parting \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxlix. 5 — \emph{let them sing aloud upon their beds} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Mark i. 35 — \emph{a solitary place, and there prayed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Tim. ii. 8 — \emph{that men pray every where} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. xcix. 6 — \emph{Samuel among them that call upon his name}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{i}\,\textbf{And the places, by the same method as the hours opposite.} The closet, the housetop, the temple, the sea-shore, the bed, the wilderness — each a place where somebody in Scripture is found praying — and then \emph{every where}, which is not a seventh place but the conclusion drawn from the six.}

\enleafn{24}{\input{fragments/en024}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xcv. 8 — \emph{harden not your heart}; Heb. iii. 13 — \emph{lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xci. 6 — the Vulgate's \emph{noonday demon}, where the BCP has \emph{the sickness that destroyeth in the noon-day} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Matt. vi. 34 — \emph{sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. lxxviii. 33 — \emph{their years in trouble} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xix. 2 — \emph{day unto day uttereth speech} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxliii. 8 — \emph{for I lift up my soul unto thee}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,⚠⚠ \textbf{This is the verse Part III mis-numbers, and here the volume gets it right.} \emph{Anni mei in luctu} stands at printed \textbf{409} under \textup{Psal. xl. 9}, where the note has to say the reference is wrong; here the same half-verse is referred correctly to \textbf{\textup{Ps. lxxviii. 33}}. So the edition proves its own misprint across three hundred and eighty pages — and it confirms, from inside the book, a reading that was otherwise established only from Brightman. \textbf{Both kept as printed.}\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textbf{Two lines here take the Vulgate against the Prayer Book, and the English follows the Vulgate.} \emph{Negotium perambulans in tenebris} and \emph{dæmonium meridianum} — the business that walks in darkness and the noonday demon — are what Andrewes wrote; Coverdale has \emph{pestilence} and \emph{the sickness that destroyeth in the noon-day}. CONVENTIONS §9 makes the BCP our crib, and yields wherever he reaches past it, as he does here.}

\enleafn{32}{\input{fragments/en032}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Heb. xiii. 20 — the epistle's closing blessing, on the God who brought again the great Shepherd \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ex. xxxiv. 6 — the LORD proclaiming his own Name to Moses in the cleft of the rock; Num. xiv. 18 — Moses pleading that same Name after the spies \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Rom. vii. 24 — \emph{O wretched man that I am} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Jon. ii. 8 — Jonah out of the fish's belly: \emph{they that observe lying vanities} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxli. 4 — the plate marks its reading as the Septuagint's \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Josh. vii. 19 — Joshua to Achan: \emph{give glory to the LORD, and make confession} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. xxxii. 5 — \emph{I acknowledged my sin unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Josh. vii. 20 — Achan's answer: \emph{indeed I have sinned} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Jer. viii. 6 — \emph{no man repented him, saying, What have I done?}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textbf{Both halves of the exchange at Ai, three lines apart.} Joshua charges Achan to \emph{give glory to the LORD and make confession}; Achan answers \emph{thus and thus have I done}. Here the charge and the confession are alike the penitent's own words, with Ps. xxxii. 5 set between them — neither half meaning in the prayer what it meant in the history. The re-cutting is the composition.}

\originalsn{34}{\input{fragments/gr034}}{\input{fragments/la035}}{\textsuperscript{i}\,27 \textup{Τὰ ἔργα}] \textup{τὸ πλάσμα} \emph{apogr.} — \emph{cf. Lat.} \textup{Figmenta}, \emph{quod ex neutro fonte alio fluere potest}\\[1pt]\hphantom{x}27–28 \emph{punct. post} \textup{παριδῇς} \emph{del. apogr.} · \textup{ὁμοίωμα}] \textup{ὁμοίωμα.} \emph{apogr.}\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,27 \textup{Figmenta}] \emph{Vulg.} \textup{opera manuum tuarum}; \emph{ex Gr.} \textup{πλάσμα} \emph{pendet, non ex textu impresso}}{27}{1}
\clearpage
\markright{34}
\setnoted{1,6,7,9,13,16,20,23,27,29}
\enleafn{34}{\input{fragments/en034}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Job xxxiii. 27 — Elihu, on the man brought back from the pit \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rom. ii. 1 — to the man who judges another and does the same; [Tit. iii. 11] — \emph{condemned of himself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Hos. xiii. 9 — the LORD to Israel: \emph{thou hast destroyed thyself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Dan. ix. 7 — Daniel in the exile, at the evening sacrifice \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Neh. ix. 33 — the Levites' confession, while the Law is read \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xxxix. 7 — David, having first been dumb with silence \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. lxxxix. 46 — Ethan: how short a time God has made men for \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,1 Cor. vi. 20 — \emph{ye are bought with a price} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Ps. lxxxix. 47 — \emph{wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{i}\,\textbf{The Greek and the Latin part company in the first line.} The Greek says \emph{thou hast chastened me for the things wherein I sinned}; the Latin gives \emph{Non recepi} and refers it to Job xxxiii. 27, \emph{it profited me not}. They are not renderings of one another. The English follows the Greek, per CONVENTIONS §6, and the Latin stands as the independent witness it is — see the note at 27 below.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textbf{A pun the English Bible cannot keep.} Andrewes asks \emph{what is my expectation} and answers \emph{Substantia mea apud te est}, then four lines later \emph{Memorare quæ mea substantia}. Both are the Vulgate — Ps. xxxviii. 8 and lxxxviii. 48 — and both turn on \textbf{substantia}, which is why the two psalms can be set one on top of the other. The Authorised Version renders the first \emph{my hope is in thee} and the second \emph{remember how short my time is}, and the join disappears.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ix}\,\textup{Figmenta} \textbf{is the evidence that this Latin column is a witness and not a shadow.} The printed Greek reads \emph{the works of thy hands}, and the Vulgate of Ps. cxxxviii. 8 reads \emph{opera manuum tuarum}; the Latin here reads neither. \emph{Figmenta} — the thing moulded — can only render a Greek text that read \textup{τὸ πλάσμα}, which is what the manuscript reads and what the printed page does not.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{42}{\input{fragments/en042}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Heb. xiii. 7 — \emph{them which have the rule over you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. iii. 15 — the first promise: the seed that bruises the serpent's head \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Deut. xxxii. 29 — \emph{O that they would consider their latter end} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. xx. 6 — the labourers found standing idle in the market-place \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xxvi. 4 — \emph{I have not sat with vain persons}; Tit. iii. 10 — a heretic, after the first and second admonition, rejected \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Job xxxi. 1 — \emph{I made a covenant with mine eyes} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Hos. ii. 6 — \emph{I will hedge up thy way with thorns}\par}\\[3pt]The Hebrew in the heading — \textup{\RL{סיג התורה}}, \emph{a fence about the Law} — \textbf{is on the printed page}, not supplied; one of the few places the 1853 let Andrewes' Hebrew stand. ⚠ \textbf{And the page ends by quoting the fence.} The last resolution is Hosea's \emph{I will hedge up thy way with thorns}, so a rabbinic phrase for the Law's protective hedge opens the page and a prophet's hedge closes it. \sethead{The Second Day}
% ---------- opening 70 | 71 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{70}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Second Day}
\originals{70}{\input{fragments/gr070}}{\input{fragments/la071}}
\clearpage
\markright{70}
\setnoted{3,5,13,16,23}
\enleafn{70}{\input{fragments/en070}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. v. 3 — \emph{in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 6 — \textbf{the work of the second day}: the firmament in the midst of the waters \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxlvii. 16 — \emph{he casteth forth his ice like morsels} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxxxv. 7 — \emph{he bringeth the wind out of his treasuries} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Lev. xxvi. 40 — \emph{if they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textbf{This is the key to the whole of Part I.} Each of the seven days opens from that day's work in Genesis, and prays out of it: the second day made the firmament, so the second day's prayer begins there and runs down through the waters above the heavens — showers, ice, dew, hail, snow, hoar-frost, winds — before it turns to confession. The days are not seven prayers that happen to fall in a week; they are the week itself, prayed through.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{78}{\input{fragments/en078}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,[Ps. xxxix. 8] — \emph{and my substance is with thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xxxi. 1 — \emph{let me never be put to confusion}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{i}\,⚠ \textbf{The same half-verse is cited twice in this book under two different numbers.} At printed 34 it is \emph{Substantia mea apud te est}, referred to \textup{Psal. xxxix. 7}; here it is the same clause referred to \textup{[Psal. xxxix. 8]}. The difference is the numbering, not the text: \textbf{xxxix. 7 is the Authorised Version's figure and xxxix. 8 the Prayer Book's}, which runs one ahead here. And the Prayer Book's figure is the one in \textbf{square brackets} — the 1853 editor's own mark for a reference he supplied. So the plate cites Andrewes' psalm on the AV's numbering and the editor cites it on the BCP's, on two pages of one book. Both stand as printed.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{82}{\input{fragments/en082}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,\textbf{Andrewes is praying for the places he himself served, under their etymologies.} \emph{The Southern Spring} is \textbf{Southwell} and \emph{the Western Monastery} is \textbf{Westminster}, as the Latin column says outright (\emph{sc. Southwell}, \emph{sc. Westmonasterii}); with St Paul's between them these are his own prebends and his deanery. \originalsn{96}{\input{fragments/gr096}}{\input{fragments/la097}}{\textsuperscript{i}\,25 \emph{voces Hebrææ Græcis respondentes in altero} στοίχῳ \emph{subjiciuntur apogr.}: \textup{\RL{יצר}} · \textup{\RL{שגגה}} · \textup{\RL{אשם}} · \textup{\RL{חטאה}} · \textup{\RL{פשע}} · \textup{\RL{עון}} · \textup{\RL{תועבה}}}{}{1}

\markright{96}
\setnoted{7,9,10,11,14,24,25,32}
\enleafn{96}{\input{fragments/en096}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 Kings viii. 47 — Solomon at the dedication, praying for those who repent in the land of their captivity \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xli. 4 — the verse of line 21 opposite, turned into the third person \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Luke xviii. 13 — the publican, standing afar off \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Tim. i. 15 — Paul, \emph{of whom I am chief} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Luke xv. 18 — the prodigal: \emph{make me as one of thy hired servants} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xxx. 9 — \emph{thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,2 Cor. vii. 11 — the seven marks of godly sorrow, which this column sets out\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{vii}\,⚠ \textbf{Under these seven Greek words for sin the manuscript sets a Hebrew column, and the 1853 left it out.} The apograph gives \textup{\RL{יצר}} · \textup{\RL{שגגה}} · \textup{\RL{אשם}} · \textup{\RL{חטאה}} · \textup{\RL{פשע}} · \textup{\RL{עון}} · \textup{\RL{תועבה}} — \emph{yetzer, shegagah, asham, ḥaṭṭa'ah, pesha, avon, to'evah}, the standard rabbinic vocabulary of sin, set as a lexicon beneath the Greek. \textbf{It is not in the printed book at all.} ⚠ And the first of them is the word Andrewes glosses \textup{\RL{יצר טוב}}, the good inclination, at printed 76: so his \emph{φαντασία} is being read through the rabbinic doctrine of the two inclinations, which is a fact about his theology and not a footnote about his text. Recorded here; not restored to the page.}
\clearpage

A dropped nought, kept as printed — the fifth place in this edition where one page corrects another.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textbf{Two verses of the same shape, set one under the other.} \emph{My sins are not hid from thee} and \emph{my groaning is not hid from thee} are different psalms — lxix and xxxviii — and Andrewes has put them together for the repeated clause, which is how most of this book is built. The English keeps both, unvaried, so the repetition reads as the design it is.}

\enleafn{134}{\input{fragments/en134}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Jas. iii. 2 — \emph{in many things we offend all} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Jas. ii. 13 — \emph{judgment without mercy to him that hath shewed no mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 John i. 8 — \emph{if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 John ii. 1 — \emph{we have an advocate with the Father} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. lxxvii. 7 — \emph{will the Lord cast off for ever?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Heb. xii. 1 — \emph{the sin which doth so easily beset us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Jas. i. 21 — \emph{superfluity of naughtiness}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{He doubles the preposition, and the doubling is the argument.} \emph{Advocatum ad te apud te habeo} — an advocate \textbf{to} thee and \textbf{with} thee: the one pleaded before is the one pleaded to, and both are God. It is the court figure the book keeps returning to, and the English holds both prepositions rather than smoothing them into one.}
\clearpage

\markright{136}
\setnoted{1,6,25,26,27,28,30,32}
\enleafn{136}{\input{fragments/en136}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 John ii. 16 — \emph{the pride of life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Matt. v. 3 — \emph{blessed are the poor in spirit; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Heb. xi. 6 — \emph{a rewarder of them that diligently seek him} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Job xix. 25 — \emph{I know that my redeemer liveth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. xvi. 16 — Peter at Cæsarea Philippi: \emph{thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,John iv. 42 — the Samaritans: \emph{this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Tim. i. 15 — \emph{of whom I am chief} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Acts xv. 11 — Peter at the council: \emph{we shall be saved, even as they}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{Three confessions in a row, and not one of them from the same quarter.} Job's \emph{I know that my redeemer liveth} comes from outside Israel altogether; Peter's \emph{thou art the Christ} from the chief of the apostles; the Samaritans' \emph{this is indeed the Saviour of the world} from foreigners who had believed on the word of a woman. Andrewes sets them one under another without comment, and the arrangement says what no one of them says alone.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{138}{\input{fragments/en138}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Job xix. 25 — the verse continuing: \emph{whom I shall see for myself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xxvii. 15 — \emph{to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. xxxiii. 20 — \emph{our soul waiteth for the LORD} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xxxiii. 21 — \emph{let thy mercy be upon us, according as we hope in thee}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,⚠ \textbf{\textup{Psal. xxvii. 15} is not an error: it is the Prayer Book's numbering.} The Authorised Version has this verse at xxvii. 13; the BCP Psalter, which divides the psalm differently, has it at 15 — and the BCP is the book Andrewes had to hand, as printed 433 shows twice over. \textbf{Do not "correct" it.} The volume moves between the two numberings without warning, and only reading the verse tells you which is in use.}

\sethead{The Sixth Day}
% ---------- opening 148 | 149 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{148}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sixth Day}
\originals{148}{\input{fragments/gr148}}{\input{fragments/la149}}
\clearpage
\markright{148}
\setnoted{3,6,9,12,13,14,16,17,18}
\enleafn{148}{\input{fragments/en148}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. lxxxviii. 13 — \emph{in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 25 — \textbf{the work of the sixth day}: the beast of the earth after his kind \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gen. i. 26 — \emph{let us make man in our image} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxxxviii. 8 — the divine hand set to its own work \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Gen. ii. 7 — \emph{and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. viii. 6 — \emph{thou madest him to have dominion} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. xci. 11 — \emph{he shall give his angels charge over thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Gen. ii. 8 — \emph{and the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{Seven dignities in the making of man, counted out.} A deliberation held beforehand, the divine hand set to the work, the breath of life, the image, dominion over the works, angels given charge, and a garden — each with its text. Andrewes is not retelling Genesis i but \emph{itemising} it, and the sixth day's prayer is built on the count: what man was made with is the ground of everything the page goes on to ask.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{150}{\input{fragments/en150}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,2 Pet. i. 4 — \emph{partakers of the divine nature} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. iii. 15 — the promise of the seed that should bruise the serpent \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gal. iv. 4 — \emph{when the fulness of the time was come} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Hos. xiii. 16 — the prophet's word of a people fallen by its own iniquity \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Hos. xiv. 2 — \emph{so will we render the calves of our lips} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Joel ii. 17 — \emph{give not thine heritage to reproach}\par}}
\clearpage

\markright{152}
\setnoted{8}
\originalsn{152}{\input{fragments/gr152}}{\input{fragments/la153}}{\textsuperscript{i}\,8 \emph{Græca om. apogr., quæ Hebraice leguntur}: \textup{\RL{ואתה תעל משחת חיי}} (\emph{Ion.} ii. 7), \emph{sub titulo} \textup{Τοῦ Ἰωνᾶ}}{}{1}
\clearpage
\markright{152}
\setnoted{1,3,8,25,26,30}
\enleafn{152}{\input{fragments/en152}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Amos vii. 5 — Amos staying the judgment: \emph{O Lord GOD, cease, I beseech thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Jonah ii. 8 — \emph{they that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Zech. iii. 3 — Joshua the high priest in filthy garments, and Satan at his right hand \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Zech. ix. 11 — \emph{by the blood of thy covenant} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. li. 2 — \emph{cleanse me from my sin}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,⚠ \textbf{Here the manuscript reads HEBREW where the printed page reads Greek.} The apograph gives \textup{\RL{ואתה תעל משחת חיי}} — Jonah ii. 7, \emph{thou hast brought up my life from corruption} — under its own heading, \emph{Of Jonah}; the 1853 set the Greek instead. This is the sharpest of the thirteen places where the printed book quietly drops Andrewes' third script, because here the Hebrew is not a gloss beside the text but \textbf{the text itself}. Recorded, not restored.}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 154 | 155 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{154}
\setnoted{}
\originals{154}{\input{fragments/gr154}}{\input{fragments/la155}}
\clearpage
\markright{154}
\setnoted{2,5,9,14,18,24,25,29,32}
\enleafn{154}{\input{fragments/en154}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Zech. iii. 2 — \emph{is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Luke xxiii. 34 — \emph{Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Acts vii. 60 — Stephen, kneeling: \emph{lay not this sin to their charge} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Luke xxii. 44 — \emph{his sweat was as it were great drops of blood} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Heb. v. 7 — \emph{with strong crying and tears} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxxix. 3 — \emph{the plowers plowed upon my back} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. xxii. 16 — \emph{they pierced my hands and my feet} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,1 Cor. xi. 24 — \emph{this is my body, which is broken for you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. lxxxv. 2 — \emph{thou hast covered all their sin}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{The Passion assembled out of five books, and not one of them a Gospel narrative of it.} The bloody sweat and the strong crying come from Luke and Hebrews, but the plowed back, the pierced hands and feet and the covered sin come from the Psalms, and the broken body from an epistle about a supper. Andrewes builds the scene from texts that are not describing it, which is why the sequence reads as prayer and not as recital.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{8,12,13,16,22,25,26}
\enleafn{158}{\input{fragments/en158}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 Cor. xii. 8 — the gifts of the Spirit, severally divided \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. cxxxviii. 8 — \emph{forsake not the works of thine own hands} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gen. i. 26 — \emph{because} in thine image and likeness \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Rev. v. 9 — \emph{because} thou hast redeemed me by thy blood \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Tit. iii. 5 — \emph{because} of the washing of regeneration \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Rom. xi. 17 — \emph{because} thou hast graffed me into the good olive tree \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Eph. v. 30 — \emph{because} a member of his body\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,*\emph{Five pleas, and every one of them begins }Quia\emph{.}* The prayer does not ask on the ground of need but on the ground of fact — because I am in thine image, because thou hast bought me, because thou hast washed me, because thou hast graffed me in, because I am a member. The repeated conjunction is the argument, and the English keeps it at the head of each line rather than varying it for elegance.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{2,3,4,5,6,7,10,12,13,14}
\enleafn{172}{\input{fragments/en172}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Matt. viii. 8 — the centurion: \emph{speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Matt. viii. 25 — the disciples in the storm: \emph{Lord, save us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Mark iv. 38 — \emph{carest thou not that we perish?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. ix. 2 — to the man sick of the palsy: \emph{thy sins be forgiven thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Luke xvii. 13 — the ten lepers, standing afar off \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Mark x. 47 — blind Bartimæus by the wayside \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Mark vii. 34 — to the deaf man: \emph{Ephphatha, that is, Be opened} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Luke xiii. 12 — to the bowed woman: \emph{thou art loosed from thine infirmity} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. xxxv. 3 — \emph{say unto my soul, I am thy salvation} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,2 Cor. xii. 9 — \emph{my grace is sufficient for thee}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{i}\,*\emph{The whole page is one request, asked ten times: }say it to me\emph{.}\emph{ Andrewes goes through the Gospels collecting the words Christ spoke to particular people — }be opened\emph{ to the deaf man, }thou art loosed\emph{ to the bowed woman, }thy sins be forgiven thee\emph{ to the palsied, }my grace is sufficient* to Paul — and asks for each of them in the first person. He is not recalling the miracles; he is asking to be the one they were said to. The Psalm and the Epistle at the foot are admitted on the same terms, as words spoken to somebody.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{184}{\input{fragments/en184}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rev. xix. 5 — \emph{praise our God, all ye his servants, both small and great} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rev. xxi. 4 — \emph{for the former things are passed away}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,⚠ \textbf{The manuscript has its largest silence immediately after this line.} Andrewes' own book leaves \textbf{three blank leaves} here — six blank pages, more than it leaves anywhere else — and the next thing in it is the great personal intercession that the 1853 prints on the following leaf. The printed page runs straight on. What the blank leaves mean is not settled: they may mark the end of the seven days, or room left for matter never written. \textbf{Nothing has been re-cut on the strength of them}; the division is recorded here and in \textup{apparatus/CLASS-B-unit-boundaries.md}, which is where a decision about it would have to be argued.}

\enleafn{202}{\input{fragments/en202}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Mark xvi. 14 — \emph{he upbraided them with their unbelief and hardness of heart} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Eph. iv. 19 — \emph{who being past feeling} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Mark iii. 5 — \emph{grieved for the hardness of their hearts} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Tim. iv. 2 — \emph{having their conscience seared with a hot iron} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Rom. i. 28 — \emph{God gave them over to a reprobate mind} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Matt. xii. 32 — the word against the Holy Ghost, which shall not be forgiven \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 John v. 16 — \emph{there is a sin unto death} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,2 Pet. i. 20 — \emph{no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,1 Tim. vi. 20 — \emph{profane and vain babblings} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,1 Tim. i. 3 — \emph{that they teach no other doctrine} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,1 Tim. vi. 4 — \emph{questions and strifes of words}\par}}

\enleafn{204}{\input{fragments/en204}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Acts xii. 22 — Herod hailed as a god, and eaten of worms \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Acts xxiv. 27 — Felix, \emph{willing to shew the Jews a pleasure} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,2 Sam. vi. 16 — Michal despising David as he danced before the ark \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Sam. ii. 13 — the fleshhook of Hophni, taking the priests' portion by force \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,2 Kings xi. 1 — Athaliah destroying all the seed royal \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Acts viii. 18 — Simon offering money for the gift; Matt. xxvi. 15 — Judas' thirty pieces \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Tim. iii. 6 — \emph{not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Hos. iv. 4 — \emph{this people are as they that strive with the priest} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,2 Sam. xv. 31 — Ahithophel's counsel, prayed into foolishness \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,1 Kings xxi. 15 — the judges of Jezreel, and Naboth's vineyard \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Num. xxv. 5 — the plague at Baal-peor \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Josh. vii. 26 — the valley of Achor, where Achan was stoned\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,\textbf{This page names disasters by a single figure and expects the story to come with it.} \emph{Hophni's fleshhook}, \emph{Michal's contempt}, \emph{Athaliah's plundering}, \emph{Ahithophel's counsel}, \emph{the judges of Jezreel}, \emph{the torrents of Belial}, \emph{the plague of Peor}, \emph{the valley of Achor} — each is one or two words standing for a whole history, and the deprecation works only if the reader supplies it. Nowhere else in the volume does so much depend on knowing what a name is for; without the notes below, the English of this page is a list of proper nouns.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{4,7,8,9,10,11,12,16,18,20,22,27,30}
\enleafn{210}{\input{fragments/en210}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Heb. xii. 28 — \emph{let us serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,2 Cor. vi. 1 — \emph{that ye receive not the grace of God in vain} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Heb. xii. 15 — \emph{lest any man fail of the grace of God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Tim. iv. 14 — \emph{neglect not the gift that is in thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Gal. v. 4 — \emph{ye are fallen from grace} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,2 Tim. i. 6 — \emph{stir up the gift of God which is in thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,2 Pet. iii. 18 — \emph{grow in grace} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,1 Thess. iii. 10 — \emph{might perfect that which is lacking in your faith} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Luke xvii. 5 — \emph{increase our faith}; Heb. iii. 6 — \emph{the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Isa. xlii. 3 — \emph{the smoking flax shall he not quench} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Rom. v. 5 — \emph{the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Jas. iv. 6 — \emph{he giveth grace unto the humble} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,Ps. lxxxvi. 11 — \emph{unite my heart to fear thy name}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textbf{Seven verbs of grace in seven lines, and they make a single argument.} Not to receive it in vain, not to fail of it, not to neglect it, not to fall from it — then to stir it up, to grow in it, to continue in it. Four negatives and three positives, each with its own epistle, mounting from the least a man can do to the most. The English keeps them as seven separate lines because the ladder is the point.}
\clearpage

\sethead{The Evening Office}

\setnoted{13,18,20,24}
\enleafn{220}{\input{fragments/en220}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. lxxi. 9 — \emph{cast me not off in the time of old age} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Isa. xlvi. 4 — \emph{even to hoar hairs will I carry you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Luke xxiv. 29 — the two at Emmaus: \emph{abide with us; for it is toward evening} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,2 Cor. xii. 9 — \emph{my strength is made perfect in weakness}\par}}

\enleafn{222}{\input{fragments/en222}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Eccl. xi. 8 — \emph{let him remember the days of darkness; for they shall be many} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Matt. xxii. 13 — \emph{bind him hand and foot, and cast him into outer darkness} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxxxiv. 2 — \emph{lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD}\par}}

% ---------- opening 224 | 225 ----------

\markright{224}
\setnoted{}
\originals{224}{\input{fragments/gr224}}{\input{fragments/la225}}
\clearpage
\markright{224}
\setnoted{2,4,8,12,15,19,20,22,23,25,27}
\enleafn{224}{\input{fragments/en224}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xlii. 10 — \emph{my prayer unto the God of my life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. lxiii. 4 — \emph{I will lift up my hands in thy name} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxli. 2 — \emph{the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Job xxxv. 10 — \emph{God my maker, who giveth songs in the night} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Isa. xxxviii. 12 — Hezekiah again: \emph{from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ecclus. v. 5 — \emph{add not sin unto sin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Prov. xxiv. 16 — \emph{a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Matt. xviii. 22 — \emph{until seventy times seven} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Jer. v. 30 — \emph{a wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Isa. xxx. 15 — \emph{in returning and rest shall ye be saved} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Deut. xxx. 2 — \emph{and shalt return unto the LORD thy God with all thine heart}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{vii}\,\textbf{Two sevens, set against each other.} \emph{A just man falleth seven times} is the measure of a day's failure; \emph{until seventy times seven} is the measure of the forgiveness asked for it. Andrewes puts them two lines apart and lets the arithmetic do the work — the second number is not merely larger, it is the first one multiplied, which is the point Christ was making to Peter.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{i}\,⚠ \textbf{\textup{Psal. xlii. 10} is the Prayer Book's figure, not a slip.} The Authorised Version has \emph{my prayer unto the God of my life} at xlii. \textbf{8}; the BCP Psalter numbers it 10. The same verse is cited the same way at printed \textbf{433}, four hundred pages later — so the book is consistent in this, and it is further evidence that the Prayer Book Psalter was physically to hand. \textbf{Do not correct it.}}
\clearpage

\markright{234}
\setnoted{12,15,17,18,19,20,22,26}
\enleafn{234}{\input{fragments/en234}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xxxi. 5 — \emph{O LORD God of truth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. xxxiii. 5 — Jacob to Esau: \emph{the children which God hath graciously given} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxxxix. 2 — \emph{thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxxi. 8 — \emph{from this time forth, and even for evermore} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. lxiii. 6 — \emph{when I remember thee upon my bed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. lxxvii. 6 — \emph{my spirit made diligent search} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. cxxxix. 18 — \emph{when I awake, I am still with thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. iv. 8 — \emph{thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety}\par}\\[3pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textbf{\textup{Ad scopandum spiritum meum} — he keeps the spade.} Ps. lxxvii. 6's \emph{my spirit made diligent search} is, in the Greek Andrewes used, a verb of digging over the ground; the evening examination is a turning of the soil, not a rummage. The same figure governs §41 in Part II, where the day's review is a \textbf{recall} of stragglers rather than a reveille. The English holds the spade in both places.}
\clearpage
